extracted.intended_audience: geometers, mathematicians, and advanced students of classical geometry
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic and geometric criteria and constructions for the common tangents to two circles (and the related Apollonian problem of inscribing polygons whose sides pass through given points). Includes classification of cases, algebraic tangency conditions, constructive proportions, and trigonometrical reductions for the inscribed-triangle case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence and number of common tangents (four-fold classification)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are generally four distinct straight lines each touching the two given circles. The page enumerates four principal cases determining how many real tangents exist:
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1. If the two circles intersect: p1 + p2 is greater than d, while |p1 − p2| is less than d; then two of the algebraic solutions are real and two imaginary — hence two real common tangents. 2. If one circle lies wholly within the other: both p1 + p2 and |p1 − p2| are greater than d and R is imaginary — no common tangent. 3. If the circles touch externally: p1 + p2 = d and |p1 − p2| < d — two tangents (and the other two coalesce to form the tangent at the point of contact). 4. If one circle lies within and touches the other internally: there is one tangent (the two algebraic solutions coalesce) and other roots are imaginary. Use these criteria (inequalities/equalities involving radii and centre distance) to classify solvability and number of real tangents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic tangency condition (quadratic must be a complete square)
rubrics_metrics.description: When substituting the line y = a x + h into the circle equation, the resulting quadratic in x must be a complete square for the line to be tangent to the circle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eliminate y between the circle equation and y = a x + h to obtain a quadratic (equation (4)). Require that this quadratic be a perfect square; this yields an explicit relation between a, h and the circle radius/centre (given by equations analogous to (5) and (6) for each circle). Use those relations for solving a and h simultaneously so the same line is tangent to both circles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportions locating intersections of tangents with the line joining centres
rubrics_metrics.description: The abscissas (positions) at which the common tangents meet the line joining the centres satisfy specific proportions relating the radii and centre separation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From eliminating parameters one obtains proportions such as H − r : H : : d : x and R : r : : d : x (as stated in the text), giving the ratios needed to find the points C and C' on the line of centres where the tangents meet. These proportions reduce the geometric construction to locating points by simple length relations on the centre line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction to tangent-from-a-point construction
rubrics_metrics.description: The general construction of the common tangents can be reduced to the classical problem: from a given external point draw tangents to a given circle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometrically, after determining the abscissas where tangents meet the centre-line one obtains points C and C'; drawing tangents from these points to suitably reduced or enlarged circles (radii R−r or R+r) produces lines parallel to the required common tangents. Thus the problem is reduced to the elementary ruler-and-compass construction of tangents from a point to a circle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplicity and degeneracy of algebraic solutions (real, imaginary, coalescing roots)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each algebraic formulation yields up to four solutions in general; special geometric configurations cause roots to be imaginary or to coalesce, changing the number of real tangents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algebraic expressions (e.g. equation (23) in the text) contain parameters p and R each taking two values giving four algebraic equations. Depending on signs and discriminants, two, one, zero or four real tangents result. When radicals disappear (discriminant zero) two tangents coalesce into a single tangent at the contact point. Imaginary roots indicate no real tangent exists in that algebraic branch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trigonometrical reduction for the inscribed-triangle Apollonius problem
rubrics_metrics.description: To inscribe a triangle MNP in a given circle so its three sides (produced if necessary) pass through three given external points A, B, C, introduce central angle variables and set up three tangent-based trigonometric equations (equations (1)–(3)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let the central angles to the required vertices be 2x, 2y, 2z and write equations of the form tan(x − m/2)/tan(x + m/2) = (a−r)/(a+r) (see text). The three resulting trigonometric equations are sufficient to determine x,y,z; they reduce algebraically to a quadratic in an auxiliary variable and hence are constructible by ruler-and-compass. Expect two possible values for each unknown (two solutions), with imaginary or degenerate cases when insoluble or reducing to first degree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological preference: geometric (Euclidean) vs analytic (Cartesian) approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: When restoring/classifying solutions of classical tangency problems, geometric (Euclidean) constructions and analyses are favored for their directness and 'Apollonian' character; analytic/trigonometric methods yield concise formulas but may obscure geometric structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical discussion recommends examining geometric constructions (porisms, lemma-based methods) for elegance and apportioning credit; analytic solutions (e.g., Lagrange's) are terse but sometimes regarded as 'condescending' simplifications. For constructive tasks, prefer geometric reductions when seeking ruler-and-compass constructions; use analytic approaches to obtain closed-form relations and algebraic reductions when beneficial.
